Backpressure is a fundamental mechanism in streaming pipelines that addresses the asymmetry between producer and consumer rates. When a downstream consumer cannot keep up with an upstream producer's emission rate, unbounded buffering will eventually exhaust memory. Backpressure solves this by allowing the consumer to signal the producer to slow down or stop.

## Common implementations

**Bounded queues with blocking**: The simplest form uses a fixed-size queue between producer and consumer. Once the queue reaches capacity, the producer's send operation blocks until the consumer drains items, creating a natural speed-matching mechanism.

**Credit-based flow control**: The consumer explicitly grants the producer permission to send a fixed number of items (a "credit"). As the producer sends items, it decrements its credit. When credit reaches zero, the producer must wait for the consumer to grant more credit before continuing. This gives the consumer fine-grained control over the flow rate.

**Reactive-pull models**: Instead of the producer pushing items to the consumer at its own pace, the consumer actively requests items on demand. The producer only sends when the consumer explicitly pulls, inverting the flow direction and giving the consumer full control over its consumption rate.

## Why it matters

Without backpressure, a fast producer paired with a slow consumer creates an ever-growing buffer that consumes memory until the system crashes. Backpressure transforms this into a stable system where the producer naturally slows to match the consumer's capacity, similar to how water pressure in a pipe prevents runaway flow.

Backpressure is central to reactive programming frameworks and modern streaming architectures (e.g., Project Reactor, RxJava, Kafka, Akka Streams) where handling variable and unpredictable consumer rates is essential.
